item.title: Micah Parsons to practice in pads on Sunday
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The Packers plan to have defensive end Micah Parsons on the field against the Rams on Wednesday night and Parsons will check off one more box toward that return to action at practice on Sunday.
item.content:encoded:
The Packers plan to have defensive end Micah Parsons on the field against the Rams on Wednesday night and Parsons will check off one more box toward that return to action at practice on Sunday.

Head coach Matt LaFleur told reporters at a press conference that Parsons will practice in pads for the first time since he got back on the practice field earlier this month. LaFleur called it "the next marker" for Parsons to clear before he gets the green light to face the Rams.

LaFleur said the team will have a plan in place for how many snaps Parsons would play in his first game since tearing his ACL last December.

“He is an elite player, he's an elite athlete. I do think you see with many of these guys — I never want to put limitations on anybody, but he hasn’t played football in a long time. You gotta be conscious of that."

The Packers will release their first injury report for Week 12 later on Sunday and injury designations for the NFL's first Thanksgiving Eve game will be released on Tuesday.

item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: Mayfield was listed as questionable due to a foot injury.
item.content:encoded:
The Buccaneers will have Baker Mayfield at quarterback for Sunday's game in Detroit.

Mayfield missed practice on Wednesday with a foot injury, but returned on Thursday and head coach Todd Bowles signaled that Mayfield would play in his Friday press conference. Mayfield is reportedly dealing with plantar fasciitis and is at risk of aggravating the injury, so Jalon Daniels could wind up factoring into the game if things take a turn for the worse.

item.title: Broncos, TV legend Tom Jackson dies at 75
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Tom Jackson, a 14-year veteran with the Broncos and a longtime fixture on ESPN's NFL programming, has died.
item.content:encoded:
Tom Jackson, a 14-year veteran with the Broncos and a longtime fixture on ESPN's NFL programming, has died. He was 75.

Jackson was a fourth-round pick of the Broncos in 1973. He became a full-time starter in his second season. He started a run of three straight Pro Bowl berths in 1977, the same year the Broncos made their first Super Bowl appearance.

Jackson played until 1986. The next year, he debuted on ESPN. He worked on the network's Sunday NFL Countdown show and the must-see NFL Primetime, which featured extended highlights packages years before the best plays could be instantly seen on social media.

"All of us are stunned," Jackson's long-time on-air partner, Chris Berman, said in a statement. "I'm stunned, we're stunned and you're stunned. We've lost one of the best human beings ever to walk the planet, Tom Jackson. I was fortunate to work side by side with Tom for 30 years, primarily on NFL Primetime and Sunday NFL Countdown. It was a labor of love for our whole team, both in front of the camera and behind it. We always hoped our viewers enjoyed the shows as much as we did bringing it to them every week."

Jackson is a member of the Broncos' Ring of Fame, the franchise's 50th anniversary team, and the Louisville Ring of Honor. He received the Pete Rozelle Radio-Television Award from the Hall of Fame in 2015.

The recent changes to the Pro Football Hall of Fame's rules could make Jackson a candidate for the expanded "contributor" category, given that it allows former players to enhance their standing with other contributions to the game. Few have combined an impactful and prolonged playing career with an impactful and prolonged broadcasting career.

We extend our condolences to Jackson's friends, family, teammates, and colleagues.

item.title: The Week 11 afternoon schedule is short on must-see games
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: As the NFL's haves and the have-nots continue to declare themselves, it's becoming challenging at times to find compelling games.
item.content:encoded:
As the NFL's haves and the have-nots continue to declare themselves, it's becoming challenging at times to find compelling games.

And while the coming week has five of them in national, standalone windows (Vikings-49ers, Packers-Rams, Bears-Lions, Chiefs-Bills, and Broncos-Steelers), the eleventh Sunday is a bit lacking. To say the least.

In the early window, three of the seven games feature double-digit spreads. The 8-1 Bills (-16.5) host the 1-8 Dolphins, who don't have their starting quarterback. The 7-2 Chiefs (-15.5) host the 3-7 Cardinals, who are down to their fourth quarterback of the season — and the third in three weeks.

The 7-2 Bears (-11.5) host the 3-6 Saints.

None of the early games feature two teams with winning records. Bucs-Lions is arguably the most compelling of the window, given the potential for Detroit stepping into a trap four days before the Thanksgiving showdown against the Bears.

The late time slot is led by the 7-2 Jaguars (-6) at the 5-3-1 Giants. It's the only game of the weekend featuring a pair of division leaders.

Having six teams on a bye this weekend doesn't help.

Although it's impossible in May to know how the various games of a given schedule will look in late November (Steelers-Eagles had the potential on paper to be the best game of the day), it's a convenient time for a subpar Sunday. With millions still scratching their GTA itch, they can fully focus on Vice City this afternoon before the Vikings and 49ers square off tonight in Mexico City.

item.title: Troy Aikman's latest comments invite speculation that he's hoping for an early exit
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: In isolation, the latest comments from ESPN's Troy Aikman about Monday night partner Joe Buck would have barely been noticed.
item.content:encoded:
In isolation, the latest comments from ESPN's Troy Aikman about Monday night partner Joe Buck would have barely been noticed. In context, they sent another shockwave through the folks who monitor the comings-and-goings of broadcasters.

Aikman's crack that Buck "always wanted a one-man booth" and the snark-oozing observation that Buck is "ubiquitous" happened two days after their mutual boss, ESPN president Jimmy Pitaro, called the media coverage of the Aikman-Buck feud "disappointing."

That was a clear message to the folks in position to add fuel to the fire: Knock it off. Aikman, in his first opportunity to speak publicly during a weekly Thursday radio segment on 96.7 The Ticket in Dallas, sprayed lighter fluid on it.

The development has sparked an uptick in speculation that Aikman will be gone not after the upcoming Super Bowl, but before it. The real question, as we see it, is whether that's what Aikman wants.

If he knows it's done after the Super Bowl, why delay? And if he can say just enough to get ESPN to choose to take the cringe out of an awkward kitchen — but not so much to be fired for cause — he gets the rest of the year off, with full pay.

Given that Aikman has well-documented aspirations to work for a team, why be tied to ESPN through Valentine's Day? If ESPN tells him to take the rest of the year off, he can immediately start looking for a landing spot in a front office.

Sure, Aikman would be giving up the chance to call a Super Bowl. But he has already called six of them. And this one will play out with increasing chatter about his future, making the perfunctory ESPN press conference during Super Bowl week a standing-room event with endless questions about the Aikman-Buck relationship and Aikman's next step.

For now, everyone will be watching and waiting. On Monday night, Aikman and Buck will be back in the booth together. Will Buck make reference to the "one-man booth" remark? If so, will Aikman take the bait?

With seven Monday night games and a wild-card broadcast to go, there will be plenty of chances for the simmer to become a boil during a broadcast. The closer it comes to happening, the more inclined ESPN may be to give Aikman what he possibly wants.

item.title: Report: Baker Mayfield dealing with plantar fasciitis
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: Buccaneers quarterback Baker Mayfield is expected to play against the Lions on Sunday, but the foot injury that led to him being listed as questionable is likely to be an issue in the weeks to come.
item.content:encoded:
Buccaneers quarterback Baker Mayfield is expected to play against the Lions on Sunday, but the foot injury that led to him being listed as questionable is likely to be an issue in the weeks to come.

Ian Rapoport of NFL Media reports that Mayfield is dealing with plantar fasciitis. The injury is believed to be a strain rather than a sprain and Mayfield spent much of the team's bye week in a boot to help his foot feel ready to go for this Sunday.

Mayfield practiced on Thursday and Friday with head coach Todd Bowles saying on Friday that the quarterback was trending in the right direction to be able to play against Detroit.

Given the nature of the injury, there is a risk that Mayfield could aggravate it and put himself at risk of missing more time. For now, though, Mayfield is planning to play through the injury with the hope that things don't get any worse.

item.title: Tyler Shough is the Saints' leading rusher, with 187 yards this season
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: As Saints quarterback Tyler Shough struggles through his second season, a good running attack could help take some pressure off him.
item.content:encoded:
As Saints quarterback Tyler Shough struggles through his second season, a good running attack could help take some pressure off him. Unfortunately, the Saints' leading rusher is Shough himself.

That might be OK if running the ball were Shough's strong suit, but he has just 187 yards rushing this season. Shough is the leading rusher in New Orleans because the Saints haven't found a running back who can establish himself as a consistent threat running the ball, not because he's doing anything special himself.

The Saints have given five different running backs a significant number of carries this season, but none has emerged as the lead back: Alvin Kamara has 49 carries for 161 yards. Kendre Miller has 57 carries for 159 yards. Travis Etienne has 38 carries for 142 yards. CJ Donaldson has 17 carries for 81 yards. Audric Estime has 22 carries for 78 yards.

Every other team in the NFL has at least one running back with more rushing yards than Kamara, the Saints' leader. Most teams have two or more. For the Saints, relying on Shough to be their leading rusher is not a successful way to run an offense.

item.title: Report: Daniel Jones is likely to wait to sign with the "right team at the right time"
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: New reporting doesn't mention the path he took in 2024 — signing with a practice squad.
item.content:encoded:
Any team can claim the contract of quarterback Daniel Jones on waivers before the Monday deadline. Given the $10.51 million injury guarantee for 2027, which becomes a full guarantee if he suffers an injury that prevents him from passing a physical by March, it's unlikely that any will.

And so he'll become a free agent, like he did after he was benched (for financial reasons) and then cut by the Giants two years ago today.

Via ESPNFL, Jones is "unlikely" to sign with another team immediately. His preference, per the report, will be to "wait for the right opportunity with the right team at the right time."

There's a cake-and-eat-it option not mentioned by the new report. Jones can sign with a practice squad, giving him the flexibility to jump to another team's active roster in the event the planets align for Jones to step in and play for a contender in relevant late-season games.

That's what he did in 2024, joining the Minnesota practice squad while keeping the ability to jump to a 53-man roster elsewhere.

Why wouldn't he do that again? It would keep him working within the confines of an NFL team, which could result in reports that he's looking much better there than he did during his 2026 season in Indianapolis, which had him dead last among all qualifying quarterbacks with a passer rating of 65.4.

Whether he chooses to do that or not, it becomes an obvious (if not likely) option for Jones. Especially since he did the exact same thing the last time he found himself benched and then released.

item.title: Steelers try for first win in Philadelphia since LBJ was president
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: October 24, 1965.
item.content:encoded:
October 24, 1965.

That's the last time the Pittsburgh Steelers won a regular-season game in Philadelphia.

LBJ was president. Bonanza was the top show on TV. Yesterday was the No. 1 song.

The Steelers entered that game 0-5. The Eagles were 2-3. Pittsburgh's quarterback was Bill Nelsen. Philly's was Jack Concannon.

The 20-14 final score was fueled by a pair of defensive scores. Willie Daniel returned a fumble 17 yards for a touchdown. Jim Bradshaw had an 82-yard interception return for another six. (He had three interceptions in the game.)

The Eagles otherwise dominated. They gained 388 yards. The Steelers gained 132. Pittsburgh fumbled five times, but recovered four of them. Running back Dick Hoak, who passed away recently, led Pittsburgh with 46 yards from scrimmage.

Since that day, the Eagles are 11-0 at home against the Steelers. Today, in a game that was flexed out of the 4:25 p.m. ET window because the Eagles are in a soft-tank free fall, the Steelers are 6-3 and the Eagles are 2-7.

For the Steelers, a loss today could see 6-3 become 6-7 quickly; their next three games are against the Broncos, the Texans, and the Jaguars.

So beyond ending a 61-year streak of futility in Philly, the Steelers need to win this one today. Even if they do, those next three games could alter the trajectory of the season and throw the Steelers into a scramble for a playoff berth in a stretch run that includes the Ravens, Panthers, Titans, and Ravens.

item.title: The Colts, as expected, won't activate WR Alec Pierce from injured reserve
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: As the Colts fully embrace the making of business decisions over the pursuit of victories, this one is no surprise.
item.content:encoded:
As the Colts fully embrace the making of business decisions over the pursuit of victories, this one is no surprise.

Via Ian Rapoport of ESPNFL, the Colts won’t activate receiver Alec Pierce from injured reserve. He'll miss the rest of the season, with the goal of being fully and completely healthy for 2027.

The situation with Pierce becomes just another one of the tangible examples of the manner in which everything has gone sideways for the Colts over the past calendar year, starting with the November 2025 trade for cornerback Sauce Gardner. Despite knowing that Pierce had an ankle issue that would eventually require surgery, the Colts re-signed Pierce at the outset of free agency to a four-year deal with an annual average of $28.5 million.

While well below the top of the market at the position, it was a major investment in a player with a significant injury. Pierce had surgery in late March and played two games in September (catching five passes for 72 yards) before landing on injured reserve due to an aggravation of the condition.

Given the timing of the deal with Pierce (it was announced just as the March 9 negotiating window opened), it appears that the Colts put a number on the table aimed at keeping him from taking a comparable deal elsewhere. With the Colts promptly trading receiver Michael Pittman Jr. to the Steelers, and in light of the limited production they've gotten from Pierce this year, it's very easy to conclude they should have let Pierce walk, keeping Pittman and moving on.

At this point, with the team at 3-8 and pivoting to quarterback Anthony Richardson Sr., there's no reason to rush Pierce back. From the moment the Colts traded guard Quenton Nelson to the Seahawks and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner back to the 49ers, the Colts threw in the shoe on 2026. Everything that has happened since then serves only to highlight the fact that they no longer care about 2026 (to the delight of the Jets, who hold Indy's first-round pick next year), and that they're trying to best position themselves for 2027.

Keeping Pierce on IR is just another obvious aspect of that broader plan. And it bolsters the possibility that owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon will decide to give coach Shane Steichen another year.

After a hard-fought Week 7 game at Minnesota saw a potential 3-4 record slip to 2-5, the "we'll get 'em next year" plan was fully activated. While Steichen can be held accountable for the first seven games, it's hard to pin much blame on him for the final ten.

item.title: NFL Playoff Picture 2026: Updated AFC and NFC standings, bracket, tiebreakers for Week 11
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: Sunday night's Vikings-49ers game is a very big one in the NFC playoff race.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL playoff race is in full swing, with the Bills and 49ers currently in the lead for the No. 1 seeds, and a huge Sunday Night Football game in Mexico City giving the Vikings a chance to pull even with the 49ers. We look at the playoff race for Week 11 below:

AFC Playoff Picture

DIVISION LEADERS

1. Bills (8-1): Heavily favored to stay on top today against the Dolphins.

2. Chiefs (7-2): Have the tiebreaker edge over the Jaguars and Bengals because of a better record in AFC games.

3. Jaguars (7-2): Their head-to-head win over the Bengals is big.

4. Bengals (7-2): In control of the AFC North.

WILD CARDS

5. Broncos (7-2): Currently behind the Chiefs based on the AFC West record tiebreaker, but that can change.

6. Steelers (6-3): Head-to-head loss to the Bengals hurts their chances in the AFC North.

7. Browns (6-4): Have a clear path to the playoffs.

OUTSIDE LOOKING IN

8. Patriots (5-5): Hard to see them competing without Drake Maye.

9. Texans (4-6): Running out of time to go on a run.

10 Raiders (4-6): The rest of the season is about developing Fernando Mendoza.

11. Ravens (4-6): Lamar Jackson's injury just about killed their playoff hopes.

12. Colts (3-8): No longer competing.

13. Jets (2-8): Aaron Glenn is on the hot seat.

14. Chargers (1-8): The NFL's most disappointing team.

15. Dolphins (1-8): The playoffs this year were never a realistic possibility.

16. Titans (1-8): Need to figure out if Cam Ward is their quarterback.

NFC Playoff Picture

DIVISION LEADERS

1. 49ers (8-1): Big game Sunday night against the Vikings.

2. Lions (7-2): Own the head-to-head tiebreakers over the Bears and Vikings.

3. Giants (5-3-1): Clear path to the playoffs in John Harbaugh's first season.

4. Panthers (4-5): Best record in the NFL's worst division.

WILD CARDS

5. Vikings (7-2): Have the head-to-head tiebreaker over the Bears.

6. Bears (7-2): Their 0-2 record in the NFC North is a concern.

7. Packers (6-4): Have the tiebreaker over the Seahawks based on their better record in the NFC.

OUTSIDE LOOKING IN

8. Seahawks (6-4): Currently have the tiebreaker edge over the Rams, but those two teams still play each other twice.

9. Rams (6-4): The preseason favorites to win it all now look like long shots to make the playoffs.

10. Cowboys (4-6): It won't be easy to catch the Giants in the NFC East.

11. Commanders (3-5-1): May need to run the table to win the division.

12. Buccaneers (3-6): Still in the race in the terrible NFC South.

13. Saints (3-6): Still in the race in the terrible NFC South.

14. Falcons (3-7): Still in the race in the terrible NFC South.

15. Cardinals (3-7): Have been more competitive than expected, but they're not going anywhere this year.

16. Eagles (2-7): The worst team in the NFC.

item.title: The first 21 chapters of Quarterback of the Future are available
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: For the 25th anniversary of the launch of PFT, I decided to post the rewritten Quarterback of the Future — one chapter per day.
item.content:encoded:
For the 25th anniversary of the launch of PFT, I decided to post the rewritten Quarterback of the Future — one chapter per day.

Three weeks in, 21 chapters are available. The full menu is here, with a button at the bottom of each chapter to quickly move to the next.

The chapters are short. Which means there are plenty of them. But each one reads quickly and, ideally, tempts the reader to read the next one.

It's the writer's job to make the reader want to do that. If you haven't started, here’s Chapter One. If you like it, click to Chapter Two.

I may accelerate the process as we get into the holiday season, possibly increasing to two or three per day.

If you want to wait until more are posted, that's fine. All chapters will remain up until all of them are posted. After that, we'll leave it up for a while, if you want to be able to read the whole thing without getting to the end of what's been released and don't want to wait.

The whole thing is a thank you to those of you who have been out there since the early days, when we didn't know what we were doing and it looked like it.

Actually, not much has changed.

item.title: Josh Allen is one score away from four straight seasons with 12 or more rushing touchdowns
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Bills quarterback Josh Allen has become something that few quarterbacks are — a rushing-touchdown machine.
item.content:encoded:
Bills quarterback Josh Allen has become something that few quarterbacks are — a rushing-touchdown machine.

In nine 2026 games, Allen has 11 rushing touchdowns. With only one more, he'll have his fourth straight season with 12 or more rushing touchdowns.

Via NBC Sports research, that would make him only the fifth player in NFL history to have four straight seasons with 12 or more rushing touchdowns.

The others were all running backs. LaDainian Tomlinson did it six times. Shaun Alexander accomplished it five times. Derrick Henry and Adrian Peterson did it four times each.

Henry, who has 10 this year, is two short of running his own streak to five seasons in a row.

Allen's next rushing touchdown will give him 91 for his career, putting him in a tie for 12th all time with Franco Harris and Jerome Bettis. Given that Allen is only in his ninth season, the all-time rushing-touchdown record of 164, held my Emmitt Smith, could eventually be in jeopardy.

item.title: Jaylen Harrell allegedly assaulted rideshare driver before crash
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The Titans announced on Saturday that defensive end Jaylen Harrell was hospitalized in Tampa after a "serious car accident."
item.content:encoded:
The Titans announced on Saturday that defensive end Jaylen Harrell was hospitalized in Tampa after a "serious car accident." It doesn't sound like it was the usual car accident.

Via WTSP, the Tampa Police Department said that Harrell was the passenger in a rideshare and that "he reportedly assaulted the driver while the vehicle was in motion."

The driver then swerved, hitting another car before colliding with a utility pole. The impact caused Harrell to be thrown forward, striking his head against the windshield and losing consciousness.

Harrell was already on injured reserve. Per the Titans' statement, he remains hospitalized.

Criminal charges are possible for Harrell, obviously. The driver suffered minor injuries in the wreck; the driver of the other car was not injured.

item.title: Knee surgery complicates Puka Nacua's future
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Timeline for recovery make mean he won't be 100 percent before free agency.
item.content:encoded:
On Friday, Rams coach Sean McVay said receiver Puka Nacua will miss "a couple months." Nacua is reportedly expected to miss a couple months more than that.

Via ESPN, the recovery time following surgery to repair the MCL tear is four to five months. If accurate, that ends Nacua's 2026 season.

The problem becomes 2027. Nacua is in the last year of his rookie contract. He hasn't gotten a second deal, due in large part to the off-field issues that recently resulted in a three-game suspension under the Personal Conduct Policy and that culminated in an offseason stay at an in-patient holistic rehab facility after he was "drowning myself" in alcohol.

Based on the ESPN report, Nacua won't be back to 100 percent before free agency starts. The Rams will have to decide whether to sign him to a new deal, to apply the franchise tag (or the transition tag), or to let him become a free agent.

The injury makes it very difficult for Nacua to land in the Jaxon Smith-Njigba ballpark ($42.15 million per year), even though Nacua's skills and abilities justify that type of deal.

The situation becomes a prime example of the extent to which off-field issues can complicate a player's financial interests. Without the New Year's Eve incident that resulted in a lawsuit and, eventually, a diversion program and, inevitably, a suspension under the Personal Conduct Policy, Nacua would have had his second contract by now. Or, at a minimum, he would have had greater standing to hold out (or hold in) until he got paid what he deserves.

Instead, Nacua continued to carry the injury risk into the final year of his rookie contract. And the injury risk became reality 13 days ago, when McVay dialed up a running play to Nacua on third and 11 while trying to run out the clock in a 20-13 game against the Commanders.

It's a win for the Rams, who may be able to keep Nacua for a lot less than it would cost to give him a market-level contract. However the Rams play the situation, Nacua's knee injury will make it easier, and cheaper, to re-sign him.

Ultimately, Nacua may have to prove in 2027 that he is back to full strength. And he may have to get through a full season unscathed to unlock the long-term deal his performances earned — but his off-field complications squandered.

Given the way he plays, it's hardly a given that Nacua will emerge from the 2027 season with the kind of performance, and health, that will finally get him the contract he should have gotten by now.

item.title: NFC North continues its historic dominance
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: They're 27-10 overall, and 21-4 in games outside the division.
item.content:encoded:
The NFC North continues to perform like no other division in the league.

Three of the teams (Lions, Bears, Vikings) have a record of 7-2 through 10 weeks. The Packers are 6-4.

The combined record of 27-10 equates to a success rate of 73 percent — the highest by any division through Week 10 in NFL history.

Outside the division, the teams of the NFC North are 21-4. The 84-percent success rate is the most for any division through Week 10 since the AFL-NFL merger.

This weekend, the Lions host the Bucs, the Bears host the Saints, and the Vikings face the 49ers in Mexico City.

In theory, all four teams could make the playoffs. That would require the fourth-place team landing higher in the standings than the second-place team in each of the other three divisions.

And that makes Wednesday night's game between the 6-4 Packers and 6-4 Rams critical to the outcome of the chase for the wild-card berths in the NFC.

item.title: Aidan Hutchinson wasn't fined for sack that injured Drake Maye
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: As expected, Lions defensive end Aidan Hutchinson wasn't fined for the tackle that may have ended Patriots quarterback Drake Maye's season.
item.content:encoded:
As expected, Lions defensive end Aidan Hutchinson wasn't fined for the tackle that may have ended Patriots quarterback Drake Maye's season.

The weekly announcement from the league includes no fines against Hutchinson.

A question emerged as to whether Hutchinson's sack of Maye amounted to a hip-drop tackle. During the broadcast, Fox rules analyst (and former NFL senior V.P. of officiating) Mike Pereira said it wasn't a hip-drop tackle. On Monday, NFL in-house rules analyst Walt Anderson confirmed that it wasn’t a hip-drop tackle.

But it's not Anderson who makes the decisions on fines. Jon Runyan makes those decisions. Not surprisingly, Runyan decided that the tackle was not a violation of the rules.

Under the rules, a hip-drop tackle happens when a player "grabs the runner with one or both hands or wraps the runner with both arms; and . . . unweights himself by swiveling and dropping his hips and/or lower body, landing on and/or trapping the runner’s leg(s) at or
below the knee." Anderson said Hutchinson did not "unweight" himself or "swivel."

Hutchinson suffered a torn ACL in his knee while celebrating the sack. Although it's not clear whether Maye will play again in 2026, Hutchinson is done for the year.

item.title: CeeDee Lamb fined $23,882 for block the league used as a highlight
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: Lamb was praised for the block by the league's website and by Tom Brady, but the disciplinary process said he used his helmet.
item.content:encoded:
When Cowboys wide receiver CeeDee Lamb made a downfield block on a George Pickens touchdown catch Sunday against the 49ers, the league's website was so impressed that the highlight video on NFL.com emphasized Lamb's block over Pickens' touchdown.

"Can't-Miss Play: CeeDee Lamb's HUGE block springs Pickens free for 39-yard TD," the caption on the highlight video says.

Calling the play on Fox, Tom Brady praised Lamb, immediately recognizing it as a great downfield block.

But the league's disciplinary process didn't think it was so great. Lamb has been fined $23,882 for what the NFL deemed "Unnecessary Roughness: Use of the helmet."

Lamb confirmed to reporters on Thursday that he had been informed he was getting fined, but he insisted he didn't make contact with his helmet and found it frustrating that receivers take hits routinely but get fined when they make one.

"I can block, and I'm real good at doing things like that, but I get fined," Lamb said. "I never touched him with my helmet. . . . I guess as a receiver, we can get hit, but can't deliver the punishment."

Lamb will surely appeal the fine for what looked, both to the league's website and the league's all-time greatest player, like a good block.

item.title: Raiders owner Mark Davis hated the Madden movie
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Did anyone read the script before allowing the Raiders' name and logo to be used?
item.content:encoded:
The new Madden movie includes a brief, fleeting glance of a young Mark Davis. The depiction wasn't flattering.

His assessment of the film is far less flattering.

The Raiders owner teed off on the Madden movie, in an interview with John Katsolimetes of the Las Vegas Review-Journal.

“My comment is, it’s full of turducken," Davis said initially.

Is that a good thing or a bad thing?

“It depends on whether you like turducken or not, and obviously, I don’t like turducken," Davis said.

His biggest concern was the script.

“I think it’s really it’s unfair to take people that have passed away and make caricatures out of them, and try to sell it as truth,” Davis said. “They start the movie with a statement saying that all of it’s not true, but some of it is, so it’s confusing what to believe.”

That's not an uncommon device. "Based on a true story" means that plenty of liberties will be taken in an effort to make the story more compelling.

Mark Davis had one specific concern regarding the shading of the truth. He objected to his father's reaction to the serious neck injury suffered by Patriots receiver Darryl Stingley, during a preseason game in 1978.

“So John goes over to the hospital afterwards, you know, and really looks after him," Mark Davis said, "and there’s a scene where my dad is telling John, ‘You don’t need to go over there. You don’t need to take care of other teams’ players. You take care of our players.'

"That’s just so far from the truth. Anybody who has ever known him knows my dad always took care of people behind the scenes. If it was a player from another team had an issue that wasn’t being taken care of, my dad would quietly take care of that even if it was players on other teams. I’m serious. . . . It just it felt cheap to me to build up John’s image at the expense of my father’s.”

Davis praised Christian Bale for his portrayal of Al Davis.

“You can’t blame the script on him," Mark Davis said. "He tried.”

Mark Davis also didn't care for the characterization of the iconic John Madden by Nicolas Cage.

“You know, he at times did look like John, but he wasn’t John," Davis said. "I mean, they made John to be a pussy, and John was the farthest thing from a pussy.”

The end result could be a positive. Mark Davis is now motivated to create something that properly and accurately depicts his father.

“I don’t know what this movie’s purpose was, to be honest," Mark Davis said. "But you know, it’s making me more and more realize that I’m going to have to put together something on my dad. It could be a movie, it could be a characterization, but at least it’ll be truthful. . . .

“I think I need to do that, or at least let people know that I’m thinking about doing that, so that don’t jump in and think that they can do it first.”

The concerns expressed by Mark Davis regarding the script raise the question of whether he or the league or anyone bothered to review it before allowing the producers to use the Raiders name, colors, and logos in the filming of the football sequences. That's a critical aspect when it comes to the overall credibility of a film about pro football.

If it looks real, it feels real. Unlike other films that didn't secure the ability to use actual team names and logos (Any Given Sunday, The Replacements).

And that's the irony of this. Davis and the league allowed the Raiders name and uniforms to be included in the film, giving it the impression of accuracy and authenticity. Which, in turn, makes the story seem accurate and authentic. Which makes it even harder to separate the truth from the fiction.

Here's hoping Mark Davis comes up with a way to tell the true story of Al Davis. With no embellishment, fabrication, or Hollywood tricks aimed at making the story seem better than it was.

Because the story of Al Davis would be pretty damn compelling if it were indeed confined to the strict parameters of reality.

item.title: Will Shane Steichen be back in 2027?
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: After the 2025 season ended, Colts owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon put both G.M.
item.content:encoded:
After the 2025 season ended, Colts owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon put both G.M. Chris Ballard and coach Shane Steichen on notice that much was expected in 2026.

Then, one day after the Colts lost to the Titans in Week 6, she fired Ballard and kept Steichen.

Nearly five weeks later, Steichen remains. After next Sunday's game against the Giants, the Colts will enter their bye. That's typically the best time for an in-season coaching change, since it gives the interim coach maximum time to get up to speed before the next game.

Creating a vacancy with six weeks left in the regular season carries a separate benefit. The team can get a head start on searching for the replacement. And if ownership already knows the coach will be fired after the season ends, it makes no sense to delay that part of the process.

So here's the question. Will Irsay-Gordon bring Steichen back in 2027?

It makes no sense to keep a new G.M. from hiring a new coach. Every G.M. arrives with a wish list of coaches who would be pursued, if/when the position is vacant. It makes plenty of sense to give a new G.M. an immediate vacancy to fill.

But what about the Colts this year has made sense? The firing of the G.M. left the team without a seasoned, experienced executive to navigate the strategy of making, or not making, trades. They quickly moved guard Quenton Nelson and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner. They rejected offers for running back Jonathan Taylor and quarterback Daniel Jones. They moved two starting receivers — Keenan Allen and Josh Downs — on the day of the trade deadline.

Now, they've abruptly released Jones.

Steichen has been operating for much of the season with one hand tied behind his back. Now, he'll have both wrists secured. Whatever the decision will be as to Steichen, it's unfair to base it on the team's overall performance since the Nelson and Buckner trades.

Before that point, they took the Chiefs to overtime in Kansas City. They beat the Texans. They manhandled the Commanders in London. They took the Vikings to the limit in Minnesota.

Although the signs point to Steichen eventually being fired, the fact that he's still there now means he could still be there later. The new G.M. may be expected to work with him.

It's ultimately the owner's call. And the owner may have strong feelings about Steichen's skills and abilities, based on the fact that she's on the sideline every week.

If she was upstairs, she'd likely be hearing criticism of the head coach during the game. Instead, she's watching him in his element. And she hasn't fired him yet.

Throw in the fact that a new coach may not be as welcoming to the owner's presence in the bench area, and she may be even more inclined to give Steichen (who's fine with it) another chance. Especially since she systematically began making his job much more difficult the moment the Colts traded Nelson and Buckner.

Moving forward, it'll be virtually impossible. The fact that Steichen has survived this long could mean that he'll survive whatever comes next.
